sec: Causes, risks & prediction of preterm birth
q: All of the following are risk factors for spontaneous preterm birth EXCEPT:
opts: A previous uncomplicated term delivery
A previous spontaneous preterm birth
A short cervical length in the second trimester
Multiple pregnancy and uterine anomalies
exp: Prior preterm birth, short cervix, multiples, infection and uterine anomalies raise risk; a previous uncomplicated term birth is reassuring.

q: Match the preventive measure with its current place — 1) Vaginal progesterone 2) Cervical cerclage 3) Bed rest and hydration … A) Offered when a short cervix is found on ultrasound, even without a previous preterm birth B) Considered with a cervical length below 25 mm and a history of mid-trimester loss or preterm birth C) Widely used but never shown to prevent preterm birth, so not recommended
exp: Progesterone treats the incidental short cervix, cerclage suits the classic history with a short cervix, and bed rest has no proven benefit.

q: Fill up: Preterm labour is regular uterine contractions with progressive cervical change occurring between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
exp: The window runs from 20 weeks to 36 weeks and 6 days; before 20 weeks the loss is called an abortion rather than preterm labour.

q: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks is in established preterm labour with intact membranes. Corticosteroids and magnesium for neuroprotection have been started. Which tocolytic is most appropriate, and for how long?
opts: Nifedipine or an oxytocin antagonist for up to 48 hours, to complete steroids and arrange transfer
No tocolytic at all, since delaying delivery never helps the baby
Indomethacin after 32 weeks, continued for seven days
Ritodrine for two weeks so that she can be managed at home
exp: Tocolysis buys up to 48 hours for steroids and transfer; indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios.

q: Fill up: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given when delivery is anticipated before ______ weeks, using a loading dose of ______ g.
exp: A 4 g loading dose followed by an infusion is given before 32 weeks and reduces the risk and severity of cerebral palsy in survivors.

q: Which of the following statements about prelabour rupture of membranes is TRUE?
opts: The earlier the gestation at rupture, the higher the risk of chorioamnionitis, pulmonary hypoplasia and cord prolapse
Rupture of membranes before labour always demands immediate delivery, whatever the gestation
Rupture of membranes at term is labelled prelabour rupture of membranes
Prophylactic antibiotics have no effect on latency and are given only for established infection
exp: At term, rupture before labour is called prelabour rupture (PROM); preterm rupture is PPROM, and antibiotics do prolong latency and reduce infection.

q: All of the following help to diagnose rupture of membranes EXCEPT:
opts: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein estimation
Sterile speculum examination showing pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix
Nitrazine or pH testing of vaginal fluid
Ferning of dried vaginal fluid seen under the microscope
exp: Pooling on speculum, an alkaline pH and arborisation (ferning) diagnose rupture; amniotic fluid tests such as AFP belong to other diagnoses.

q: A woman at 34 weeks with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is afebrile, with a normal CTG and normal inflammatory markers. What is the management?
opts: Expectant management with antibiotics, corticosteroids and close monitoring, planning delivery around 34-37 weeks
Immediate caesarean section to avoid infection
Induction of labour within twelve hours, whatever the gestation
Discharge home on oral antibiotics with weekly outpatient review
exp: Expectant care with antibiotics and surveillance balances prematurity against infection; delivery is timed by gestation and any sign of infection or compromise.

q: Match the feature with its significance in chorioamnionitis — 1) Maternal fever 2) Fetal tachycardia 3) Uterine tenderness with offensive liquor … A) A baseline above 160 bpm, often an early and easily missed fetal sign B) A core temperature of 38 C or more with maternal tachycardia C) Clinical evidence of intrauterine infection requiring delivery and intravenous antibiotics
exp: Maternal fever plus fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor form the clinical triad that demands delivery and antibiotics.

q: Fill up: Post-term pregnancy is defined as a gestation of ______ weeks or more, and the added fetal risk comes mainly from ______.
opts: 42; placental insufficiency and oligohydramnios
40; fetal macrosomia alone
41; fetal anaemia and hydrops
42; congenital malformation
exp: Beyond 42 weeks the ageing placenta may fail, liquor falls and the risk of meconium, macrosomia and stillbirth rises.

sec: ACOG management of post-term pregnancy & macrosomia
q: A 34-year-old with an uncomplicated pregnancy reaches 41 weeks and 3 days. The CTG is normal and the amniotic fluid index is 9 cm. What is the recommended management?
opts: Offer induction of labour between 41 and 42 weeks, with increased fetal surveillance if she chooses to wait
Reassure her and await spontaneous labour until 43 weeks without intervention
Immediate caesarean section, because post-term fetuses never tolerate labour
Admit for daily amniocentesis to test fetal lung maturity
exp: Induction is offered from 41 weeks because perinatal risk falls; membrane sweeping and increased monitoring are options while she waits.
